## Purpose
Two deterministic layers. `RevisionApplyLayer` carries the edit operations out on a copy of the base. `RevisionNormaliseLayer` then repairs the invariants the edits left inconsistent and refreshes the run inputs.

## Responsibilities
- **`RevisionApplyLayer`** (`label="Make the edits"`):
  - `ops.apply_operations(base, operations, repair=False)` sets `spec.proposed` and `spec.outcomes`;
  - with no summary, the summary is the notes of the successful outcomes, at most 600 chars;
  - **if nothing was applied**, the revision fails with "None of the edits could be made: <reasons or 'there was nothing to apply'>". The exception is a code-fix-only turn (code fixes and no operations);
  - the layer summary is "N of M edit(s) applied[ — K could not be: …]".
- **`RevisionNormaliseLayer`** (`label="Keep the graph whole"`):
  - its notes are `ops.normalise(proposed)` + `ops.dangling_references(proposed)` + `repair_layer.finalise_inputs(proposed)`;
  - the summary is the notes, or "Nothing needed repairing.".

## Key elements
The two classes.

## Control flow
As above.

## Data, state and side effects
Mutates the proposal on the revision spec only.

## Configuration
None.

## Interactions
- **Uses:** `app.workflow_revisions.operations` and `repair_layer.finalise_inputs`.

## Error handling and edge cases
See above.

## Nuances and gotchas
Applying does what was asked. Normalising guarantees the planned-workflow invariants (no links to missing steps, groups that converge, an entry step that exists) whatever was asked. They are separate promises, so they are separate layers.
